To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

language dominance, not first language, influenced the use and effectiveness of semantics in non-native listeners’ recognition of English sentences, and that syntax was the most important factor in non-native listeners, native English monolingues, and non-native listeners’ sentence recognition.

the relative weighting of semantics and syntax in sentence recognition is different for native and non-native listeners and that language dominance influences the use of semantics but not the use of syntax.
non-native listeners do not utilize semantics as effectively as native English listeners and that language-dominance influences the use of semantics in English sentence recognition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relative weight of semantic and syntatic cues in sentence recognition by native and non-native English listeners.
how language background affects the use and weighting (or relative contribution) of semantic and syntactical cues to speech recognition in English.
the relative weighting of semantic and syntax in the context of speech recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relative weight of semantic and syntactical cues in sentence recognition is a function of the language background of the listener.
the use of semantic and syntactical cues in sentence recognition in noise is not only language-dependent, but also language-dominance-dependent.
the non-native listeners in the current study did not use the same amount or the same kind of contextual information to recognize English sentences in noise as the native listeners did.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
non-native listeners do not use contextual cues to the same extent or as effectively as native English listeners.
non-native listeners, even those with English as a first language, do not utilize semantic information in English as effectively as native English listeners.

the use of contextual cues in English sentence recognition is influenced not only by language background but also by dominance of a first language and that the use of both semantics and syntax in sentence recognition can be quantified via j and k factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

language background, language dominance, and first language influence the use and weighting contextual cues to recognize sentences, and that a native language advantage exists in the effective use and weighting of both semantic and syntactically cues combined.
non-native listeners, even those who have been living in an English-speaking country for a long time, are not able to use semantic cues as efficiently as native listeners.
the use of semantics is more complex than previously thought, and that the language-dominance factor should be considered in the study of semantic cue use.
